implementation_notes: Kotlin on the JVM should use java.util.concurrent, exactly as Java does; kotlinx.coroutines' Mutex is the Kotlin-shaped answer and it is a blocking (suspending) mutex, not a lock-free primitive. Kotlin/Native (the new memory model since 1.7.20) does allow free-threaded access to state and provides kotlin.concurrent.AtomicInt/AtomicLong in the standard library, which is a real atomic surface on Native. Kotlin Multiplatform code that needs the same algorithm across targets should target the platform's provided concurrent collections rather than writing the algorithm once - the memory model differences between JVM, Native and JS make a shared hand-rolled implementation impractical.
idiom_name: java.util.concurrent on the JVM; kotlin.concurrent.AtomicInt on Kotlin/Native; kotlinx.coroutines Mutex for cooperative exclusion
pitfalls: coroutines' Mutex is blocking (suspending), not lock-free - do not claim a progress guarantee from it.
Kotlin/Native's old memory model froze threads at field access, so pre-1.7.20 Native code cannot do this at all; check the language version.
kotlinx.atomicfu's atomic are inline classes and are unboxed at call boundaries, so they cannot be put in a generic collection without boxing.
Holding a Mutex across a suspension point is legal but a cancelled coroutine holding it is a deadlock risk unless released with withLock rather than manual acquire.
alternative: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex for suspending mutual exclusion, or a Channel for hand-off - both are the idiomatic Kotlin answer
